subject: Communication
title: WWI Propaganda: The Birth of Modern Persuasion
description: A short lesson to help you apply WWI Propaganda: The Birth of Modern Persuasion.

hook.text: Uncle Sam pointed at you and said 'I Want YOU.' Four million Americans enlisted.

buildup.text: World War I was the first war where governments systematically used mass media to shape public opinion and recruit soldiers.

discovery.text: The Committee on Public Information, led by George Creel, used posters, films, and speakers to manufacture war support.

twist.text: Edward Bernays, Creel's protégé, later applied wartime propaganda techniques to peacetime — inventing modern public relations.

climax.text: WWI proved that mass media could manufacture consent on a national scale. Every war since has followed that playbook.

punchline.text: Propaganda was born in war. It thrived in peace.

quiz.question: Who applied WWI propaganda techniques to create modern public relations?

details.summary: World War I saw the first systematic government propaganda campaigns. Britain's Wellington House and America's Committee on Public Information used posters, films, and staged events to manufacture public support. These techniques became the foundation of modern advertising and PR.
details.whyItMatters: WWI propaganda invented techniques still used in advertising, politics, and social media. Recognizing their origins helps you spot them today.
takeaways: WWI created the first systematic government propaganda
Techniques included posters, films, and staged events
These methods became the basis of modern advertising and PR

faq.question: How did WWI propaganda influence advertising?
faq.answer: Edward Bernays, nephew of Freud and a CPI member, directly transferred wartime persuasion techniques to commercial advertising after the war. He coined the term public relations to avoid the negative connotations of propaganda. His methods are still used in marketing today.

faq.question: What made WWI propaganda so effective?
faq.answer: It combined emotional appeals with mass media reach for the first time. Posters used vivid imagery and simple slogans. Films showed staged atrocities. Government endorsement lent credibility. Most people had never encountered coordinated persuasion campaigns and had no defenses against them.
